Today is August 12, 2026.

Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI just launched Grok Bot, but the most interesting part isn’t simply that it can create AI workers.

Each user gets a dedicated cloud computer shared across their Grok Bots. Those Bots can have different jobs, pass work between each other, create new long-lived Bots, and even run on different underlying models over time.

That leads to a much bigger idea: your future “job” may not be one AI model or one agent. It could be a persistent cloud computer that accumulates tools, context, responsibilities, and increasingly capable AI workers.

That’s my interpretation, not an xAI claim, but Grok Bot gives us a fascinating look at what that architecture could become.

#Grok #ElonMusk #AI #FutureOfWork #gigaqian

These AI workers can create new, long-lived AI workers, and they all share the same computer. I'm Giga Chen, and today I'm going to help you understand what that really means. Now creating other AI agents isn't new. Claude, OpenAI, Kimi, and others have versions of that idea. Grokbot packages it differently. That matters. SpaceX AI calls each bot a durable AI teammate with a name, a job, its own conversation, and working context that develops over time. And if you look into their documentation, it says that an existing bot can actually create another focus bot when a job needs a long-term owner. So you could have an expense manager, a recruiting bot, and even a chief of staff bot coordinating the others. They can message each other, pass work, and even assign ownership. Cutting edge? They share files, browser sessions, app logins, and even credentials used by software on that computer. SpaceX AI even explicitly warns, don't use separate bots as a security boundary. So they're not isolated employees with separated access. Why build it this way? Handoffs. A bot leaves behind something, another picks it up. It's starting to look less like an agent swarm and more like a digital office. And here's the part people are missing. These AI workers aren't even attached to one AI model. creator: gigaqian
caption:
AI-designed viruses sound terrifying, but these were bacteriophages, meaning viruses that infect bacteria.

A phage is just short for bacteriophage. A genome is the complete set of genetic instructions inside an organism or virus. A mosaic descendant is a later virus whose genome contains pieces inherited from multiple parent phages after recombination.

Researchers used AI to design new phage genomes, tested them in the lab, and found viable designs. Some later recombined into mosaic descendants during experiments. We are now seeing specialized AI models being used to build complex, interrelated systems!

The cinematic visuals in this video were made with SeeDance 2.5 to explore a more unusual use case for AI video generation. They are illustrative entertainment, not scientifically exact renderings, and should not be treated as factual depictions of molecular structures or experimental events.

#AI #biotech #science #ainews #gigaqian
transcript: One of the AI design viruses everyone's talking about today did something much stranger than simply work. It made a biological component swap that previous attempts by researchers had failed to make work. And after this video, you're going to understand what that means. I'm Giga Chen, and I want this to be the most informed community on the whole platform. But I also want you all to be entertained. So I used Higgs Field to generate some visuals using Cdance 2.5, which you all know is one of my favorite video models. And I really want to hear what you think. First, one important correction to the news cycle. The big experiment we're all talking about was actually released as a preprint last September. What's new is that the peer reviewed paper was published in Science yesterday. The researchers used a tiny bacteriophage called Phi X 174. A bacteriophage is just a virus that infects bacteria. Its genome has 5386 DNA letters and 11 genes. But here's the problem. Some of those genes overlap. The same stretch of DNA can help encode multiple proteins. So changing one letter to improve one thing can accidentally break something else. And it's not like they asked Claude or GPT to make them a virus. Rather, they fine-tuned EVO 1 and EVO 2 on 14,466 related phage sequences, guided them towards Phi X 174-like genomes, filtered the results for things like genome structure and which kind of bacteria they should infect, and then physically tested a bunch of designs. 16 of them produced viable phages. Now here's the part I don't see a lot of people talking about. One of them, EVO 536, used a DNA packaging protein called J from a distantly related phage called G4. Researchers had previously tried to deliberately engineer this kind of swap, and it didn't work. But inside this AI-generated genome, it did. When researchers looked at EVO 536 using cryo-electron microscopy, they found that this shorter protein was sitting inside a different orientation within the virus's protein shell. None of this means that AI understood why its solution worked. But it does mean that whole genome generation landed on a combo that satisfied the constraints. And the human design swaps didn't. They failed. One more critical nuance. When scientists challenged three E. coli lines that evolved resistance to Phi X 174, the winner wasn't one of those original 16. If you don't already, Andre Carpethy, one of the co-founders of OpenAI, released a loop engineering system that works when you give AI a goal and it works towards it by itself. It tries to change and test whether the results get better. Keeps it if it did, throws a weight if it didn't, and tries the next idea all automated. But here's a problem nobody noticed. Even good loops have bad habits. AI has instincts about what kinds of ideas to try. It keeps going back over the same instincts over and over even after they stop working. Your loop runs 500 experience, but it's really running the same 10 ideas 50 times. This is a fix that Frontier Lab scientists found out. You just add a second loop on top of the first one. The inner loop is the worker. It keeps running experiments exactly like before while the top loop is the coach. The coach does not do any of the work. Its only job is to watch the worker. The coach in the outer loop rewrites the worker's playbook, changing the way it searches for ideas and then setting it back in. Researchers tested this on the same exact benchmark that Carpethy used, and this new Tula version scored five times better than a single loop with the same exact LLM models. The entire improvement came from the structure that one AI is forcing the other AI to explore ideas that normally its instincts would have skipped. Melvin Conway sent this to Harvard Business Review in 1967 and they rejected it for not proving its thesis. Datamation ran it a year later. The claim: any organisation that designs a system produces a design that copies that organisation’s own communication structure. Four teams building a compiler ship a compiler with four parts.
The elaboration the video does not make: engineers now use this deliberately and call it the reverse Conway manoeuvre. Decide the architecture you want first, then arrange the teams to match, because the mirroring happens either way and the only real choice is whether it happens on purpose.
Your customers are holding a physical copy of your org chart, and they experience it as friction. Which handoff in your product is really two teams that barely speak?

#startupfounder #processdesign #leadership #teambuilding #decisionmaking
transcript: In 1967, a computer scientist called Melvin Conway noticed something strange enough that he wrote it up and sent it to Harvard Business Review. They rejected it on the grounds that he hadn't proved his thesis, so he sent it to a computing magazine instead, and they published it in 68. And the idea became one of the most quietly confirmed observations in how organizations work. Any company that designs a system will produce a design that copies the company's own communication structure, not as a metaphor, but literally. Four teams building a compiler will ship a compiler with four parts. A company where two departments barely speak will ship a product where two components barely connect. The organization chart leaks into the product piece by piece, whether anyone intends it or not. I told the Sony story a while ago, three divisions invading incompatible music players on the same stage, and Conway is the law underneath it. The customer ends up holding a physical copy of your internal politics. The reason is almost obvious, once said out loud. People design what they can talk about, and they can only talk across the channels that exist. If the channel between two teams is thin, the connection between their two components will be also thin and awkward and late. The lens that follows is the sharp part, and modern engineering systems and teams use it deliberately. Design the organization for the product you want, because you're going to ship your organization chart either way. So look at your own product honestly. Which gap in it is actually a gap between two of your teams?

creator: algo.andre
caption: Shell sort solves insertion sort’s biggest problem #code #algorithms
transcript: Shell Sort is an optimized version of Insertion Sort, and what makes it faster is a pretty clever change. Insertion Sort works by scanning the list, comparing each number to the one before it. If it's smaller, it slides backwards until it hits a number smaller than itself. But when a small number starts near the end of the list, it can only move back one step at a time, which makes Insertion Sort slow on large unsorted arrays. Shell Sort fixes this by comparing numbers that are separated by a gap. It runs Insertion Sort on these spaced-out subsequences, allowing small numbers to move large distances across the list much earlier. The gap is reduced with each pass until it reaches one. By then, the list is already mostly sorted, so a final Insertion Sort pass quickly finishes the job. So by introducing gaps...
